doc.title: Stefon Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2020

title: Sight versus ear and Wayne Shorter not reading music
summary: Harris discusses avoiding looking at the instrument, the gala story with Shorter and Herbie Hancock where Shorter said he stopped reading music, and ear training through solfeggio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Nice. I think you should write your own reviews. Getting back to improvising for a moment, when we play the saxophone or the trumpet we’re not seeing the notes. We’re knowing what key we put down, what we’re going to get. Is there a sense of sight involved when you improvise? Because the whole thing is laid out in front of you and of course your ear is the main driver I would say, but what role does sight play?

Well it’s interesting. In many ways, of course I appreciate sight, but it’s a distraction in a lot of ways because you can look down and you can see a shape and you can decide to play that shape but maybe that’s not what the music is asking for. Music is really a science of sound. So the primary way that we should be receiving information is through our ear. So for me a lot of times, especially when I’m playing a ballad, when I’m live in concert what I tend to do is I stand up really straight when I’m playing a ballad and I find a point in the back of the room. Usually there’s an exit sign that’s red or something that you can see. And I’ll just focus on that. And I’ve tried not to look down at my instrument at all, so that I’m focused more on hearing and feeling and then capturing the note that’s in my ear first. Not that there’s anything wrong with recognizing a pattern and playing that, but my ambition is to really continue to deepen my ability to see the world of sound through my ear. A great story is something that happened to me that really solidified my perspective is a couple of years ago I got a chance to play with Wayne Shorter and Herbie Hancock, we did this big gala and I was nervous of course. So the night before Don Beasley who was the musical director, he said, “Hey Stefon, do you want to write an arrangement on this tune?” I said, “Oh my goodness, of course.” So I stayed up all night, I’m writing this arrangement and we had rehearsal the next day. I come into rehearsal and I had my little charts, and I go over to Herbie, you know, I go over to the bass player. And then when I go over to Wayne Shorter, I’m, “Mr. Shorter, here’s the chart.” Wayne just says, he’s like, “Yeah, yeah, I don’t read music. I stopped reading music like seventeen years ago.” He was like, “Once my eyes got a little funny I just stopped.” And I was just thinking oh my goodness, all this beautiful music this guy has been making for the last seventeen years has all come from his incredible ability to perceive using his ear, and that it just reminded me that what we have on paper is just drawings. It’s not the actual lake. Right? You need to get out there and swim or do you want to focus on the painting? I think both are beautiful, but that was a pivotal moment for me and it reminded me that I really need to continue to develop my empathy, my ability to perceive what’s happening around me. So I would tell you probably 98 percent of the time that I’m dealing with music trying to learn, I sing — I practice solfeggio and I’m at the piano, I almost never practice at the vibes at this point. Because it’s very physical and I have a lot of muscle memory from over the years. But it’s a lot of singing, away from any instrument, just to develop my ear.
